"title": "Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions in TbB4",
"authors": "T. Inami, K. Ohwada, Y. H. Matsuda, Z. W. Ouyang, H. Nojiri, D. Okuyama, T. Matsumura, and Y. Murakami",
"field_subfield": "Condensed matter physics; magnetic materials and magnetism",
"type_of_paper": "Research letter",
"executive_summary": "This letter reports resonant magnetic x-ray diffraction (RMXD) experiments on the Shastry-Sutherland-lattice rare-earth tetra-boride TbB4, performed under strong pulsed magnetic fields up to 29 T at the SPring-8 BL22XU undulator beamline. The central motivation is that TbB4 exhibits a multi-step magnetization process above 16 T when the field is applied along the c-axis, yet this curve is difficult to predict because TbB4 has an XY-type ground state. The authors observed the intensity of the (100) magnetic reflection as a function of field and found that the magnetization plateau phases are accompanied by large in-plane (XY) components of the magnetic moments, contrary to the usual expectation that plateau phases contain only moments parallel or antiparallel to the field. A simple spin model is then deduced and used to calculate the magnetization curve. The model assumes an XY ground state with in-plane anisotropy E and excited Ising spins with energy gap D, and reproduces the one-half magnetization plateau. The key theoretical insight is that frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior, so that frustration is the key to understanding the transitions. The work integrates RMXD using brilliant third-generation synchrotron radiation with pulsed-magnetic-field techniques to explore magnetic structures at high fields close to 30 T. The study concludes that frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism, common to TbB4 and the previously reported CsFeCl3, even though the spin models for the two magnets are quite different. The paper emphasizes that the integration of two advanced experimental techniques enables exploration of magnetic structures at high fields near 30 T, which will be widely applied in the near future to the high-field phases of many interesting magnets. The research context draws on prior work on magnetization plateaus in Ising antiferromagnets, Heisenberg spins, isolated dimers, and geometrically frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets, all of which share the feature that plateau phases have collinear magnetic structures with no ordered moment perpendicular to the field. The novelty of TbB4 is that its plateau phases contain ordered perpendicular components, making it a rare class of magnets characterized by ordered perpendicular components in the plateau phase. The methodological details describe the single crystals grown by the floating zone method, the pulsed magnet with a 0.6 ms pulse duration, the avalanche photodiode detector with a 10 microsecond resolution, and the estimation of the true sample temperature by measuring the temperature dependence of the magnetic peak intensity. The procedures and architectures describe the spin Hamiltonian, the finite-size cells with periodic boundary conditions, the parameter sets J1 = 2, J2 = 1, J3 = 2, D = 1, and the limit E to infinity. The key results report that the net diffraction intensity is about 2x10^5 counts/s, the one-half magnetization plateau is visible between 20 and 24 T, the diffracted intensity of the one-half plateau structure is about one-quarter of the ground state, and the observed intensity is about 30 to 50% of the intensity at 0 T. The interpretation and theoretical implications argue that the plateau phases consist of very hard XY-type magnetic moments and Ising-like magnetic moments, and that frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields. The contradictions and limitations note that the proposed spin model is very much simplified, that interactions further than J3 must be included to account for the splitting at Hc1, and that the model captures basic features but is simplified. The claims section states that the plateau phases include the (100) component, that the large (100) component consists of the ab-plane components, and that frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism. The data and code availability note that the data are an average of 30 field-scans, and the robustness and ablation notes mention that similar results were obtained with other sets of parameters and different cell sizes. The ethical considerations note that the sample surface was locally heated by irradiation of synchrotron x-rays, and the true sample temperature was estimated. The key figures and tables describe Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3, and Figure 4. The top influential citations include the Shastry-Sutherland lattice paper, the resonant anomalous x-ray scattering book, and the pulsed-field x-ray diffraction paper. The three takeaways highlight the core contribution, the strongest evidence, and the future path."

summary.title: Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions in TbB4
summary.authors: T. Inami, K. Ohwada, Y. H. Matsuda, Z. W. Ouyang, H. Nojiri, D. Okuyama, T. Matsumura, and Y. Murakami
summary.field_subfield: Condensed matter physics; magnetic materials and magnetism
summary.executive_summary: This letter reports resonant magnetic x-ray diffraction (RMXD) experiments on the Shastry-Sutherland-lattice rare-earth tetra-boride TbB4, performed under strong pulsed magnetic fields up to 29 T at the SPring-8 BL22XU undulator beamline. The central motivation is that TbB4 exhibits a multi-step magnetization process above 16 T when the field is applied along the c-axis, yet this curve is difficult to predict because TbB4 has an XY-type ground state. The authors observed the intensity of the (100) magnetic reflection as a function of field and found that the magnetization plateau phases are accompanied by large in-plane (XY) components of the magnetic moments, contrary to the usual expectation that plateau phases contain only moments parallel or antiparallel to the field. A simple spin model is then deduced and used to calculate the magnetization curve. The model assumes an XY ground state with in-plane anisotropy E and excited Ising spins with energy gap D, and reproduces the one-half magnetization plateau. The key theoretical insight is that frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior, so that frustration is the key to understanding the transitions. The work integrates RMXD using brilliant third-generation synchrotron radiation with pulsed-magnetic-field techniques to explore magnetic structures at high fields close to 30 T. The study concludes that frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism, common to TbB4 and the previously reported CsFeCl3, even though the spin models for the two magnets are quite different. The paper emphasizes that the integration of two advanced experimental techniques enables exploration of magnetic structures at high fields near 30 T, which will be widely applied in the near future to the high-field phases of many interesting magnets. The research context draws on prior work on magnetization plateaus in Ising antiferromagnets, Heisenberg spins, isolated dimers, and geometrically frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets, all of which share the feature that plateau phases have collinear magnetic structures with no ordered moment perpendicular to the field. The novelty of TbB4 is that its plateau phases contain ordered perpendicular components, making it a rare class of magnets characterized by ordered perpendicular components in the plateau phase. The methodological details describe the single crystals grown by the floating zone method, the pulsed magnet with a 0.6 ms pulse duration, the avalanche photodiode detector with a 10 microsecond resolution, and the estimation of the true sample temperature by measuring the temperature dependence of the magnetic peak intensity. The procedures and architectures describe the spin Hamiltonian, the finite-size cells with periodic boundary conditions, the parameter sets J1 = 2, J2 = 1, J3 = 2, D = 1, and the limit E to infinity. The key results report that the net diffraction intensity is about 2x10^5 counts/s, the one-half magnetization plateau is visible between 20 and 24 T, the diffracted intensity of the one-half plateau structure is about one-quarter of the ground state, and the observed intensity is about 30 to 50% of the intensity at 0 T. The interpretation and theoretical implications argue that the plateau phases consist of very hard XY-type magnetic moments and Ising-like magnetic moments, and that frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields. The contradictions and limitations note that the proposed spin model is very much simplified, that interactions further than J3 must be included to account for the splitting at Hc1, and that the model captures basic features but is simplified. The claims section states that the plateau phases include the (100) component, that the large (100) component consists of the ab-plane components, and that frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism. The data and code availability note that the data are an average of 30 field-scans, and the robustness and ablation notes mention that similar results were obtained with other sets of parameters and different cell sizes. The ethical considerations note that the sample surface was locally heated by irradiation of synchrotron x-rays, and the true sample temperature was estimated. The key figures and tables describe Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3, and Figure 4. The top influential citations include the Shastry-Sutherland lattice paper, the resonant anomalous x-ray scattering book, and the pulsed-field x-ray diffraction paper. The three takeaways highlight the core contribution, the strongest evidence, and the future path.

Research Context
Magnetization plateaus are a hallmark of several magnetic materials, where magnetization keeps a constant value at a finite range of magnetic fields. The zero compressibility of plateaus is ascribed to the fact that Sz is a good quantum number, while a variety of mechanisms give rise to plateaus. Ising antiferromagnets exhibit the most comprehensible easy-axis magnetization, such as the one-third magnetization plateau of CoCl2·2H2O. Multi-step magnetization curves of PrCo2Si2 and CeSb are also classified into the Ising category. Magnetization plateaus are observed not only for Ising spins but also for Heisenberg spins, including isolated dimers. Cs3Cr2Cl9 and Ba3Mn2O8 exhibit three-step and two-step magnetization curves, respectively, for S=3/2 and S=1 dimers. In SrCu2(BO3)2, superstructures of excited triplet dimers are stabilized and one-eighth, one-fourth, and one-third plateaus are observed. Geometrically frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets also frequently exhibit magnetization plateaus, such as triangular- and pyrochlore-lattice antiferromagnets. For triangular- and pyrochlore-lattice antiferromagnets, one-third and one-half plateaus are observed, respectively. In real magnets, additional mechanisms stabilize the plateau phase, such as four-spin exchange coupling, quantum fluctuations, single-ion anisotropy, and magnetoelastic coupling. A crucial point is that all plateau phases have a collinear magnetic structure, with no ordered magnetic moment perpendicular to the magnetic field. Recently, a multi-step magnetization curve was observed in TbB4, which resembles none of the above-mentioned magnets.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the multi-step magnetization process of TbB4 can be understood, given that TbB4 has an XY-type ground state. The origin of the multiple successive transitions is not easily understood, because the metamagnetic behavior suggests low-lying Ising excited states just above the XY ground state. The hypothesis is that the magnetization plateau phases are accompanied by large XY components of magnetic moments, contrary to the usual collinear expectation. The predicted outcome is that the plateau phases include the (100) component in their magnetic structures. The hypothesis is that the magnetic structures in the plateau phases consist of very hard XY-type magnetic moments and Ising-like magnetic moments. The predicted outcome is that frustration is the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization. The hypothesis is that frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior. The predicted outcome is that frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism, common to TbB4 and CsFeCl3.

Methodological Details
The experiments were resonant magnetic x-ray diffraction (RMXD) experiments on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice TbB4. The experiments were carried out under strong pulsed magnetic fields up to 29 T. The experiments were performed at undulator beamline BL22XU at SPring-8. The x-ray energy was tuned to the Tb LIII absorption edge (7.514 keV). Magnetic fields up to 29 T were generated using a small pulsed magnet (20 mm in outer diameter and 24 mm in length). The pulse duration is about 0.6 ms. The magnet is a split-pair, and two windows are prepared for incoming and outgoing x-rays. The magnet and a sample were attached to the cold head of a conventional closed cycle refrigerator. Single crystals of TbB4 were grown by the floating zone method. The scattering plane was horizontal, and the a*axis was in the plane. Magnetic fields were vertical and parallel to the c-axis. A high-counting-rate detector, an avalanche photodiode, was used, and diffraction intensity was measured as a function of time with a typical resolution of 10 microsecond.

The field strength was also monitored as a function of time, and the field dependence of the diffraction intensity was obtained from these two series of data. The sample surface was locally heated by irradiation of synchrotron x-rays. The true sample temperature was estimated by measuring the temperature dependence of the magnetic peak intensity at each irradiation intensity. The net diffraction intensity is about 2x10^5 counts/s, which is marginally strong enough for a pulsed-field experiment. The intensity of the (100) reflection appears below TN1 and is constant below TN2. The field dependence of the (100) reflection at 18 K is shown in Fig. 3(c), and the data are an average of 30 field-scans. The intensity decreases with increasing magnetic fields above 16 T and keeps a constant value between 20 and 24 T, where the one-half magnetization plateau is observed. The plateau phases consist of very hard XY-type magnetic moments and Ising-like magnetic moments. The frustration nature of the SS lattice lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior. Frustration is not only an origin of degenerate states, but also breaks degeneracy. The basic scenario that frustration lifts the degeneracy at a metamagnetic transition is common for both TbB4 and CsFeCl3. Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism. The proposed spin model captures basic features of the real TbB4, even though it is very much simplified. The spin models for TbB4 and CsFeCl3 are quite different, but the basic scenario is common.
